newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Private sector revives abandoned Zambian mines.
newsitem.headline: Private sector revives abandoned Zambian mines.

text.p: Zambia's old, abandoned mines are slowly being stirred back to life by private companies.

The mining sector, already boosted by the privatisation of Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines, is expected to grow considerably as foreign mining companies revive mining operations closed as unprofitable years ago.
These include the British-owned Reunion Mining, Canada's Colossal Resource Corp and First Quantum Minerals Ltd, and the locally-owned Kabwe Power and Metal Company.
The old Bwana Mukwaba Mine has been reopened by First Quantum Minerals after being closed by ZCCM in 1984.
Feasibility studies of the mine by Bateman Minerals and Industrial Ltd of South Africa determined it has a tailings reserve of 8.4 million tonnes at 0.73 percent copper.
First Quantum will begin site preparations next month under a Zambian subsidiary, Bwana Mkubwa Mining Ltd.
Bwana Mukubwa director Kwalela Lamaswala said the project is viable at a production rate of 9,954 tonnes of copper a year.
"It is expected that Bwana Mukubwa will start production by April 1998," Lamaswala said.
Reunion Mining, meanwhile, expects to start gold production in May at the recently reopened Dunrobin mine in central Mumbwa.
"We should have started production earlier but we have had to reschedule it due to the bad wet season," said Reunion subsidiary Dunrobin Mining Ltd managing director Neil Moloney,
"We are hoping to process 720,000 tonnes of material in the first year, 50 percent of that being ore," Moloney said.
The gold content in the ore is about 2.5 grams per tonne.
And Colossal started cobalt production from ZCCM slag in the central town of Kabwe late last year, making its first sale of 12 tonnes of cobalt material in November.

The Colossal-owned Qasim Mining Enterprises Ltd processes slag with an average cobalt content of 0.8 percent up to eight percent, which is then granulated in South Africa to 15 percent cobalt content.
The company will soon install an induction smelting furnance to enable it to granulate the cobalt material locally.
It expects to process between 4,000 and 6,000 tonnes of slag per month in its first year, producing around 50 tonnes of cobalt material per month.
Meanwhile, former employees of the ZCCM lead and zinc mine in Kabwe, which closed in 1994, have reopened it and are already producing limited amounts of ore.
Kabwe Power and Metal Company produced about 400 tonnes of lead in the past three months, exporting most of it to neighbouring Zimbabwe.
"After a rehabiliation exercise, hopefully by 1998, the plant will be able to produce 1,000 tonnes of zinc and 800 tonnes of lead per month," company spokesman Kizito Mumbi said.
Exploration and prospecting activity in Zambia's mining sector is also increasing.
Mines minister Christon Tembo said about 20 foreign companies spent about $20 million in the search of new minerals last year, compared to around $2 million annually before 1991.
The privatisation of ZCCM has meanwhile gained momentum with the government inviting bidders for final negotiations on the sale of eight of the company's nine privatisation packages.
Earlier this year, Avmin Ltd signed an option agreement on the development of the Konkola North mine and aims to delineate ore resources there of around 100 million tonnes.
A consortium led by Anglo American Corp of South Africa have agreement to develop the Konkola Deep mine.
The Konkola ore development is seen as crucial to the future of Zambia's mining sector as reserves at the main Nchanga open pit are likely to run out by the end of the century.
Mining is the heart of the Zambian economy, earning around 90 percent of the country's foreign reciepts.

Output in the mining sector increased marginally in 1996, with copper production rising to 313,900 tonnes from 307,800 tonnes in 1995. Cobalt production increased to 4,830 tonnes from 2,934 tonnes in 1995.
